newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA MAY DETAIL NEW MEDIA LAWS SOON.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA MAY DETAIL NEW MEDIA LAWS SOON.

text.p: The Australian government may announce changes to the cross-media ownership laws as soon as Tuesday, a government official said on Monday.
The issue was on the agenda to be considered by Cabinet on Tuesday and it was possible the government would make a final decision about changes to the current system, he said.
"The reason it's only possible is that it's a pretty heavy cabinet agenda ... and also as you would expect, this is an issue on which every person wants to have their say," the official said.
"It's entirely feasible that they may not have time tomorrow with all the other stuff to finalise a position."

Prime Minister John Howard returned to work on Monday after a three-week bout of pneumonia to face a two-day cabinet meeting looking at tax reform, unemployment, and industry policy as well as changes to the media ownership laws.
The government official said cabinet's primary concern on Monday was tax reform. Changes to the cross-media ownership laws were not due for consideration until Tuesday, he said.
Under the current laws, television owners are banned from owning more than 15 percent of a newspaper in the same major market and vice versa.
The Liberal-National coalition government ordered a closed review of ownership limits after winning power in March 1996.

Media analysts have been alert to any signals that the government may be about to change media policy as it could affect the ownership of newspaper publisher John Fairfax Holdings Ltd and Seven Network Ltd.

Media barons Kerry Packer, who owns Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd, and Rupert Murdoch, the executive chairman of global media group News Corp Ltd, have lobbied Prime Minister Howard in recent months about the proposed changes.

Packer's PBL has a 15 percent stake in Fairfax, behind the 22 percent held by Brierley Investments Ltd of New Zealand, and has said it wanted to merge with Fairfax, possibly as soon as Christmas this year.

Murdoch has a 15 percent stake in Seven, the second ranked television group behind Packer's Nine Network, and has talked about raising the stake. Murdoch's newspaper interests in Australia are also enormous, accounting for about 70 percent of circulation in the major capital cities.
